<reason>Both sides argued the motion as written and progressed cleanly, but A found and held the decisive fulcrum: the operative clause "no reduction in base pay" in sectors where hours literally are output. A's pounce on B's overtime-threshold concession [A2.1-A2.2] forced B into a genuine dilemma — either the fifth shift disappears (service rationed) or it stays and gets ~25% dearer (taxpayer/patient pays) — and B answered honestly rather than escaping it, admitting the carer's real gain is a premium plus a norm that "pulls down over a generation" [B4.3-B4.4]. A then converted that into the cleanest weighing line of the debate: the statute is redundant where slack exists (market already delivering) and harmful where it bites. B's best offensive line, the coordination problem and "the sequence has a name: never," was strong and memorably put, but A pre-empted it with a concrete alternative path (sectoral bargaining, German 35-hour precedent, scheduling/procurement law), so B's characterisation of A as defending a permanent freeze was partly inaccurate by the time it was deployed. A also correctly showed that the historical analogies (eight-hour day, weekend, overtime) drop the very clause at issue — a statutory guarantee that nominal pay not adjust — which B never squarely answered beyond "society judged it worth it." B's "who pays today, in endurance" reframe was genuinely valuable and kept the debate close, but it establishes that the status quo has costs, not that the mandate has the capacity or funding to deliver a four-day week to the workers it was pitched to help. Both openings ran over and were clipped; B was clipped three times including its closing, which slightly blunted its final crystallisation.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's exploitation of B's concession that employers "simply pay overtime or hire" [A2.1-A2.2]: it split the motion into either lost service or a routed 25% cost shock, and forced B to concede in [B4.3] that the carer still works five shifts, with the mandate's delivered content reduced to a premium plus generational drift — which A crystallised as "redundant where it works, harmful where it bites."</best_rebuttal>
